questions.stem: Why are coal, oil, iron ore and gold classed as non-renewable resources?
options: They are destroyed completely when they are used
They form over geological time, far slower than we use them
They are found only in a few countries, so supply is limited
They cannot be recycled once they have been extracted
questions.explanation: These resources took millions of years or more to form, so they are not replenished on any human timescale. Some, such as iron and gold, can be recycled, and being found in few places does not make a resource non-renewable.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes how black coal forms?
options: Swamp plants build up as peat, are buried, and heat and pressure turn them to coal
Marine plankton settle on the deep sea floor and are buried there until they turn into coal
Hot fluids rise through cracks in rock and deposit coal as they cool
Volcanic ash builds up in layers and is compressed into coal over time
questions.explanation: Coal starts as plant material in waterlogged swamps, where low oxygen stops it decaying fully, forming peat. Burial raises the temperature and pressure, driving off water and gases and concentrating carbon. Marine plankton are the usual source of oil and gas, not coal.

questions.stem: As coal is buried deeper and longer, it passes through lignite (brown coal), sub-bituminous and bituminous coal to anthracite. What changes along this sequence?
options: The coal becomes younger and closer to the surface
The carbon content falls as more plant material is added
The carbon content and energy per kilogram increase
The water content increases and the energy per kilogram falls
questions.explanation: Higher temperature and pressure drive off water and volatile compounds, so the coal's carbon content and energy content rise from lignite to anthracite. Brown coal, such as that of Victoria's Latrobe Valley, is wet and has less energy per kilogram than black coal.

questions.stem: Where do oil and natural gas usually come from?
options: Forest plants buried in swamps and squeezed slowly by the overlying rock
Gases from volcanic eruptions trapped beneath layers of lava
Groundwater that reacts with limestone deep underground
Organic matter from marine plankton buried in fine sediments and heated
questions.explanation: Microscopic marine organisms settle in fine muds with little oxygen, and their remains are buried. Heat over millions of years converts the organic matter to kerogen and then to oil and gas. Land plants in swamps mostly form coal.

questions.stem: A geologist finds a rich organic shale that has never been buried deeply. Why is it unlikely to have produced oil or gas?
options: It has not been heated enough to turn its organic matter into hydrocarbons
Organic shales can only ever form coal, never any oil or natural gas
Oil forms only in igneous rocks, never in sedimentary shales like this one
Its organic matter was too young to contain any carbon
questions.explanation: Organic matter must be buried deep enough to reach a range of temperatures, the oil window, before it breaks down into oil and gas. Too little heat leaves it as kerogen; much more heat produces gas. Shales are the usual source rocks for oil and gas.

questions.stem: Banded iron formations, the source of much of the iron ore mined in the Pilbara of Western Australia, are layered sedimentary rocks deposited more than 2 billion years ago. How did they form?
options: Iron meteorites struck the sea floor and were buried in sediment
Iron in plants was buried in swamps and later concentrated by heat
Dissolved iron in seawater met oxygen and settled out as iron oxide layers
Molten iron from the mantle rose up through cracks and cooled in thin layers
questions.explanation: Early oceans held dissolved iron. As oxygen from photosynthesising microbes built up, the iron formed insoluble oxides that settled out in layers with silica. This shows how such deposits record conditions in Earth's early oceans and atmosphere.

questions.stem: In which geological setting are coal, oil and gas found?
options: Volcanic island arcs
Sedimentary basins
Granite intrusions
Mid-ocean ridges
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels form from organic matter buried with sediments, so they occur in sedimentary basins such as the Bowen and Sydney basins for coal and the Gippsland and Carnarvon basins for oil and gas. Igneous settings lack the organic material.

questions.stem: Much of Western Australia's gold, including that mined around Kalgoorlie, is found in ancient igneous and metamorphic rocks. How does this kind of gold deposit usually form?
options: Gold forms from buried plant material under heat and pressure
Gold grows slowly in deep soils from the decay of organic matter
Hot fluids carrying dissolved gold deposit it in veins
Gold settles slowly out of seawater onto the ocean floor in layers
questions.explanation: In lode or reef deposits, hot, mineral-rich fluids move through faults and fractures in the rock and deposit gold, often with quartz, as they cool or react. That is why gold is linked to igneous and metamorphic terrains and to major fault zones.

questions.stem: Gold has also been found as nuggets and grains in old stream gravels in central Victoria. How do such alluvial deposits form?
options: Bacteria in stream beds turn dissolved iron into gold over time
Weathering frees gold from veins and streams concentrate the dense grains
Gold crystallises directly from river water as it evaporates in summer
Volcanic eruptions spread fine gold grains across whole river valleys as ash
questions.explanation: When gold-bearing rock weathers and erodes, the gold is carried by streams. Gold is very dense, so it settles where the water slows, collecting in gravels and on bedrock. These deposits are found downstream of the original reefs.

questions.stem: For an oil or gas field to form, which combination of rocks is needed?
options: A granite body, a porous seal rock and a layer of volcanic ash
A coal seam, a limestone reservoir and an open fracture to the surface
A source rock, a porous reservoir and an impermeable seal over a trap
A source rock, an impermeable reservoir rock and a porous seal above it
questions.explanation: Hydrocarbons form in a source rock, migrate upward into a porous, permeable reservoir such as sandstone, and are held there by an impermeable seal such as shale in a structure like an anticline or fault trap. Without a seal they escape to the surface.

questions.stem: A company is exploring a region of very old granites and greenstones with no sedimentary cover. Which resource would it be most sensible to explore for there?
options: Black coal
Natural gas
Crude oil
Gold
questions.explanation: Gold deposits are associated with igneous and metamorphic terrains, where hot fluids moved through faults. Coal, oil and gas need organic-rich sedimentary basins, which this region lacks. Matching the resource to the setting saves exploration effort.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a remote sensing technique used in mineral exploration?
options: Breaking rock samples from outcrops with a geological hammer
Satellite imagery that maps rock types by the light they reflect
Diamond drilling to bring up a continuous rock core
Collecting soil samples on a grid for chemical analysis in a laboratory
questions.explanation: Remote sensing gathers data without touching the ground, from satellites, aircraft or drones. Different minerals reflect different wavelengths, so satellite images can map rock types and alteration. Drilling and soil or rock sampling are direct sampling methods.

questions.stem: An aircraft flies a survey measuring small variations in Earth's magnetic field. Which deposit would this survey detect most readily?
options: A sandstone holding natural gas
A body of magnetite iron ore
A seam of brown coal
A layer of rock salt
questions.explanation: Magnetite is strongly magnetic, so it distorts the local magnetic field and shows up clearly in aeromagnetic data. Coal, salt and gas-bearing sandstone are only weakly magnetic, so other methods, such as seismic surveys, are used for them.

questions.stem: Seismic reflection surveys send sound waves into the ground and record their echoes from rock layers. What are they mainly used for?
options: Detecting gamma rays from potassium, uranium and thorium in rocks
Measuring how strongly rocks are magnetised near the surface
Mapping buried structures such as folds that could trap oil and gas
Measuring the gold content of ore samples collected at the surface
questions.explanation: Sound waves reflect from boundaries between rock layers, so seismic data build a picture of the structure underground, revealing anticlines, faults and other possible traps. Gamma rays are measured in radiometric surveys and magnetism in magnetic surveys.

questions.stem: A gravity survey finds a small area where the pull of gravity is slightly stronger than in the surrounding region. What could this indicate?
options: A reservoir of natural gas trapped in porous rock
A body of dense rock or ore, such as a metal sulfide deposit
A thick layer of low-density sediment, such as a coal basin
A large cave system or open void beneath the surface
questions.explanation: Gravity is slightly stronger above denser material, so a positive anomaly can point to a dense ore body. Low-density sediments, voids and gas-filled rock all reduce the local gravity, giving a negative anomaly.

questions.stem: After remote sensing identifies a promising area, why is drilling still needed?
options: To confirm the resource and measure its grade and extent directly
To produce the satellite images used to choose drill sites
To remove the ore before the company has been granted a mining licence
To measure the magnetic field from above the deposit
questions.explanation: Remote sensing and geophysics show where anomalies are, but only samples of the rock itself prove that a resource exists. Drill cores and chips are assayed to measure the grade, and a grid of drill holes maps the deposit's size and shape.

questions.stem: Drill holes on a grid across a gold prospect show ore averaging 2.0 grams per tonne in a body estimated at 5.0 million tonnes. About how much gold does the deposit contain?
options: 10 tonnes
2.5 tonnes
100 tonnes
1.0 tonne
questions.explanation: Mass of gold = grade × ore mass = 2.0 g/t × 5.0 × 10⁶ t = 1.0 × 10⁷ g = 10 tonnes. Dividing the tonnage by the grade gives 2.5 tonnes. Grades are measured from drill samples, so the estimate is only as good as the sampling.

questions.stem: Soil samples collected on a grid show unusually high copper concentrations in one area, centred over a ridge. What is the best next step?
options: Begin open-pit mining over the anomaly immediately
Abandon the area, as soil copper shows the ore has eroded
Repeat the soil sampling on the same points to confirm it
Drill beneath the anomaly to test for a deposit at depth
questions.explanation: A soil geochemical anomaly suggests metal-bearing rock nearby, but it does not show the grade or size of any deposit. Drilling tests what lies beneath. Mining without drilling risks a large loss, and an anomaly is a reason to look closer, not to abandon the area.

questions.stem: What does the grade of an ore describe?
options: The hardness of the rock that must be broken to mine it
The concentration of the valuable metal or mineral in rock
The depth below the surface at which the ore body is found
The age of the rock that contains the valuable mineral
questions.explanation: Grade is the amount of the useful metal or mineral per unit of ore, such as grams of gold per tonne or the percentage of iron. Together with the size and depth of the deposit, grade decides whether mining it will be economic.

questions.stem: An airborne radiometric survey measures gamma rays coming from the ground. What does it detect?
options: Echoes of sound waves reflected from boundaries between buried rock layers
Small differences in the pull of gravity over dense and light rock bodies
Variations in Earth's magnetic field caused by magnetic minerals in rock
Natural radioactivity from potassium, uranium and thorium in rocks
questions.explanation: Different rock types contain different amounts of the radioactive elements potassium, uranium and thorium, so radiometric maps help geologists map rock types and find uranium deposits. Sound echoes are seismic data, and gravity and magnetic surveys measure other properties.

questions.stem: Why is open-pit mining used for some deposits and underground mining for others?
options: Open pits are used only for coal, and underground mines only for gold
Open pits are used only where there is no groundwater at all
Open pits suit large, shallow deposits; underground mining suits deep ones
Open pits suit small, deep deposits; underground mining suits shallow ones
questions.explanation: Removing overburden to reach ore is affordable when the deposit is large and close to the surface. For deep or narrow, high-grade ore bodies, tunnels and shafts disturb less rock. The choice depends on depth, shape, size and grade, not on the commodity alone.

questions.stem: Most Pilbara iron ore is extracted from open pits, while some high-grade gold veins are extracted from deep underground mines. Which factor best explains the difference?
options: Iron ore is too heavy to lift out of underground mines by any method
Gold is only found below 1000 m, while iron ore is only found above it
Open pits can only extract metals that are magnetic, such as iron
The iron ore bodies are huge and shallow; the veins are narrow and deep
questions.explanation: Large, shallow bodies of ore make open pits economical, as huge volumes can be moved cheaply. Narrow, deep veins would need enormous amounts of waste removed from above, so tunnels are cheaper. Depth limits for gold and iron are not fixed.

questions.stem: Offshore oil and gas fields, such as those in Bass Strait, are produced from platforms. What does the 'completion' of a well involve?
options: Drilling the first exploration hole to find out if oil is present
Sealing and abandoning the well once the field is exhausted
Refining the oil on the platform into petrol and diesel
Fitting casing, cement and equipment so the well can produce safely
questions.explanation: After a well is drilled, it is completed: steel casing is cemented in place to protect surrounding rock and aquifers, and the well is perforated and fitted with equipment to control the flow. Exploration comes before this, and abandonment at the end of the well's life.

questions.stem: A coal seam lies 15 m below the surface across a wide area, while another lies 400 m deep. Which extraction methods are most likely for each?
options: Underground mining for the shallow seam; open-cut mining for the deep one
Offshore drilling for the shallow seam; open-cut mining for the deep one
Open-cut mining for both, as coal is always mined from the surface
Open-cut mining for the shallow seam; underground mining for the deep one
questions.explanation: A shallow, extensive seam can be reached by stripping the thin overburden, which is cheaper. At 400 m the overburden is far too thick to remove, so the coal is reached by shafts or drifts and mined underground, for example by longwall methods.

questions.stem: Coal seam gas is extracted by drilling wells into coal seams and pumping out groundwater. Why must the water be removed?
options: The water reacts with the coal to make the gas, so it must be replaced
Lowering the water pressure lets the gas held on the coal be released
The water would freeze in the pipes and stop gas reaching the surface
The water is needed for cooling the drilling equipment at the surface
questions.explanation: In coal seams, methane is held on the coal surfaces by the pressure of the surrounding water. Pumping out water reduces the pressure, so the gas is released and flows to the well. The extracted 'produced water' is often salty and must be managed.

questions.stem: In mining, what is overburden?
options: The fine waste left after the valuable mineral has been extracted
The extra weight of ore that a haul truck is not allowed to carry
The soil and rock above a deposit that must be removed to reach it
The ore that is left behind in a mine after it has been closed
questions.explanation: Overburden is the material over the top of a deposit. In open-pit and open-cut mines it must be stripped away first, so its thickness strongly affects cost. The fine waste left after processing is called tailings.

questions.stem: An open pit must remove 12 million tonnes of waste rock to extract 3 million tonnes of ore. A second deposit of the same grade needs 30 million tonnes of waste removed for 3 million tonnes of ore. Which statement is correct?
options: The first has a stripping ratio of 4 and is cheaper to mine per tonne of ore
The first has a stripping ratio of 0.25 and is dearer to mine per tonne of ore
The second has a stripping ratio of 4 and is cheaper to mine per tonne of ore
Both have the same stripping ratio, because their ore tonnages are equal
questions.explanation: The stripping ratio is waste divided by ore: 12/3 = 4 for the first and 30/3 = 10 for the second. Moving less waste for each tonne of ore makes the first deposit cheaper to mine. Dividing ore by waste gives 0.25, which inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: Some natural gas is held in rock with very low permeability, so it barely flows to a well. How is this gas extracted?
options: Fluid is pumped in at high pressure to crack the rock so gas can flow
The rock is heated until it melts, releasing the gas to the surface
The rock is dug out in an open pit and crushed to release the gas
Seawater is pumped in to dissolve the rock and carry the gas upward
questions.explanation: Hydraulic fracturing pumps water, sand and additives into the well at high pressure, opening small fractures that the sand props open, so gas can move to the well. If casing or cement fails, fluids or gas could reach aquifers, which is why well integrity is monitored.

questions.stem: What causes acid mine drainage?
options: Acid rain falling on mine sites and then washing into nearby streams
Acids used in ore processing being stored in open tanks
Limestone in the waste rock dissolving slowly in rainwater
Sulfide minerals like pyrite reacting with air and water to form acid
questions.explanation: Mining exposes pyrite and other sulfides to oxygen and water, producing sulfuric acid. The acid dissolves metals from the rock, and the drainage can harm streams for decades. Limestone does the opposite: it neutralises acid.

questions.stem: A mine pumps large volumes of groundwater out of its pit to keep it dry. Which effect on the surrounding area is most likely?
options: The water table rises, flooding nearby farmland with fresh groundwater
The groundwater becomes saltier only far from the mine
There is no effect, as groundwater is separate from surface water
The water table falls, drying springs, wetlands and deep-rooted plants
questions.explanation: Dewatering creates a cone of lowered water table around the pit. Springs, wetlands and vegetation that depend on groundwater can dry out. Groundwater and surface water are connected, so streams fed by groundwater can also lose flow.

questions.stem: How can clearing land for an open-cut mine affect a nearby river?
options: The river's flow becomes steady, as floods can no longer occur
More runoff carries sediment into the river, making it turbid
Less runoff reaches the river, so its water becomes clearer
The river's water becomes colder, as the land no longer shades it
questions.explanation: Without vegetation, rain erodes exposed soil and waste rock, and sediment washes into waterways. Turbid water blocks light for aquatic plants and smothers habitats on the river bed. Sediment control dams and revegetation reduce this effect.

questions.stem: Longwall mining removes a wide panel of coal deep underground. Months later, cracks appear in the bed of a creek above, and its flow disappears in places. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Acid from the coal dissolved the creek bed, making it disappear
Subsidence of the ground above cracked the rock, draining water downward
The coal removed from below absorbed water from the creek above
Heat from the mine evaporated the creek water through the rock
questions.explanation: When coal is removed, the overlying rock sags into the space, so the surface subsides and rock layers crack. Water can then drain from the creek into the cracks. This is an example of extraction changing a hydrologic system far from the mine entrance.

questions.stem: Produced water from coal seam gas wells is salty. If it were released untreated into a freshwater creek, which effect on the ecosystem would be expected?
options: Salt-intolerant plants and animals would decline as salinity rose
The creek would support more species, as salt adds nutrients
Only the abiotic factors would change; organisms would be unaffected
The water temperature would rise sharply, killing all aquatic life
questions.explanation: Raising salinity changes an abiotic factor that many freshwater organisms cannot tolerate, so sensitive species decline and the community changes. This shows how a change to one abiotic component affects the biotic components. Produced water is treated or stored for this reason.

questions.stem: Tailings are the finely ground waste left after ore is processed. Why are tailings dams carefully engineered and monitored?
options: The tailings could catch fire and burn for years if they dry out
The tailings are valuable and must be guarded against any theft
Tailings absorb carbon dioxide, so their area must be measured
A leak or failure could release toxic material into soils and waterways
questions.explanation: Tailings can contain fine particles, metals, acid-forming sulfides and processing chemicals. Seepage can contaminate groundwater, and a dam failure can bury habitats and poison rivers. Liners, monitoring bores and stable designs reduce these risks.

questions.stem: Which practice reduces the long-term impact of a mine on ecosystems after it closes?
options: Rehabilitation: reshaping, adding topsoil and revegetating the site
Exploration: drilling more holes to find other nearby ore bodies
Dewatering: pumping groundwater out of the pit indefinitely
Stockpiling: leaving waste rock heaped and exposed to the weather
questions.explanation: Rehabilitation restores a stable landform, puts back stored topsoil and replants local species, so the site can again support habitat and protect water quality. Leaving waste rock exposed allows erosion and acid drainage to continue.

questions.stem: Offshore drilling can release drilling fluids and occasionally oil. Why can an oil spill near the coast harm many organisms at once?
options: Oil dissolves completely in seawater within hours, raising its salinity
Oil raises the water temperature, which affects only coral reefs
Oil coats feathers, fur and gills and spreads through food webs
Oil sinks immediately and affects only animals on the sea floor
questions.explanation: Floating oil coats seabirds and marine mammals, reducing insulation and buoyancy, and smothers intertidal life. Toxic compounds pass into plankton and up the food web. Oil mostly floats and spreads; it does not dissolve completely.

questions.stem: Before mining, scientists record water quality and invertebrate species in streams both upstream and downstream of a proposed mine, and keep recording after mining starts. Why include the upstream sites?
options: They act as controls, showing changes not caused by the mine
They show how much ore is present beneath the stream bed
They are the only sites where mining can affect the water
They give a larger sample, so the downstream sites can be skipped
questions.explanation: Comparing sites above and below the mine, before and after it starts, separates the mine's effects from natural changes such as drought, which affect both. Upstream sites are not affected by the mine's discharges, which is what makes them useful controls.
